To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the Argentine estancias were not the “plantations” of the Pampas that they are sometimes portrayed to be, (2) the Argentine estancia economy was not as profitable as it is sometimes portrayed to be (and, indeed, was not profitable in the nineteenth century), and (3) there was a shortage of labor on the Argentine estancia, which is the opposite of the conclusion of Amaral.

(1) there is a positive correlation between land prices and the number of land transactions, (2) the price elasticity of the land market is positive, (3) land prices are positively correlated with the number of landowners, (4) the price elasticity is higher in more developed areas, (5) the price elasticity decreases with the size of the farm, and (6) the price elasticity does not change with the age of the owner.

(1) the estancia system of cattle raising in the nineteenth-century Pampas was profitable, (2) the profitability was due to the high productivity of the system, (3) the high productivity was due to the use of slave labor, and (4) the use of slave and free labor was determined by economic considerations, not social relations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the history of the Pampas and with the history of labor.
the social and economic structure of the estancias of Buenos Aires Province.
the social, economic, and cultural history of the Pampas in the colonial and post-colonial periods.
